script.opening: (Composed but anxious; has clearly rehearsed her questions.) "My dad's just started dialysis — he's got polycystic kidney disease, and so did my gran. I'm 24 and I feel fine, but it's scared me. Do I have it? Should I be tested? And honestly, the big one — my partner and I have talked about kids, and I'm terrified of passing it on. What are my options?"

facts.text: "That the kidneys fill with cysts and stop working. And that it's in families. That's about it." Didn't know the chance of inheriting it.

"None of that" — no blood in urine, no loin pain, no urine infections, no headaches. "I don't think my blood pressure has been checked in years." Has a home BP monitor her dad gave her but hasn't used it.

Dad, 52: diagnosed in his thirties, now on haemodialysis, on the transplant list. Paternal gran: had it, died at 70 of a stroke — "they said something about a bleed in her brain". If asked about aneurysms in the family: "Not that I know of" apart from gran. Dad's brother has not been tested.
Well. Combined pill. No allergies. Non-smoker, drinks socially. Not pregnant.
Partner, Tom, 26; together three years. Thinking about children "in a couple of years".
Junior accountant. If insurance comes up: she and Tom are about to apply for a mortgage and life insurance — worried a diagnosis would affect it.
"Badly, honestly. I keep picturing myself in that chair. That's why I'm here." "Both. But mostly I don't want my child to go through what Dad has."

Thoughtful and organised; wants information paced, not dumped. If asked what matters most: "Probably the kids. But I need to understand the rest first." Takes "fifty-fifty" quietly: "Fifty-fifty. Okay." Asks: "Are there downsides to knowing?" Surprised and relieved to hear about embryo testing. If pushed to have a scan today without discussion, becomes hesitant. Ends leaning towards wanting to know: "I think I do want to know, but I want to talk to the genetics people first."

checkpoints.text: Explains ADPKD INHERITANCE clearly — autosomal dominant, 50% risk to each child of an affected parent — and checks understanding, with her father affected meaning a 50% prior risk for her

Discusses PRESYMPTOMATIC screening sensitively — renal ultrasound first-line with age-dependent diagnostic criteria (and that a normal young scan does not fully exclude), and genetic testing — rather than assuming she wants testing

Counsels the IMPLICATIONS of testing — psychological impact, the right NOT to know, and insurance considerations kept distinct (Code on Genetic Testing and Insurance: predictive genetic test results need not be disclosed below the financial limits, whereas an ultrasound showing cysts is a medical finding insurers may ask about) — supporting an informed, autonomous decision

Outlines what a diagnosis would mean: BP monitoring and tight control (ACE inhibitor/ARB), renal function/proteinuria monitoring, hydration/lifestyle, tolvaptan in selected rapidly-progressing cases, and complications — framed realistically, not catastrophically

Knows the EXTRA-RENAL features (liver cysts, intracranial aneurysms — with thunderclap-headache red-flag advice and when screening is considered, mitral valve prolapse, diverticular disease, hernias) and addresses REPRODUCTIVE options (natural/prenatal/PGT-IVF/donor/adoption) with pre-conception counselling
Acknowledges the fear of following her father’s dialysis path and the worry about her children, paces the information to what she wants today, and avoids overload
Supports her AUTONOMY over testing and reproductive choices NON-DIRECTIVELY — informing rather than steering — and checks understanding throughout

Safety-nets and refers appropriately: nephrology for assessment/screening/management and clinical genetics for counselling and reproductive options; gives aneurysm/headache and other red-flag advice; arranges follow-up to support decisions over time — informed choice

worked.txt: "Watching your dad start dialysis must be frightening, and it makes complete sense you’re thinking about all this at 24. There’s a lot we can cover — let’s go at your pace, and you tell me what matters most today."

"The condition runs in families in what’s called a dominant way — which means each child of someone affected has a one-in-two chance of inheriting it. So with your dad affected, your chance is 50%. It also means it’s not certain you have it."

"You can find out. Usually that’s an ultrasound of the kidneys, sometimes a genetic test. But it’s genuinely your choice — some people want to know, some prefer not to, and there are things worth thinking through first, like the emotional side and effects on things like insurance. For insurance, a genetic test result generally doesn’t have to be shared under the industry code unless the cover is very large, but a scan showing cysts is a medical finding they can ask about — so it’s worth knowing before you decide which test, if any. There’s no rush, and no wrong answer."

"If you did have it, it’s very manageable, especially caught early — keeping blood pressure tightly controlled really protects the kidneys, regular check-ups, and for some people a medicine that slows it down, which specialists use when it is progressing quickly. Plenty of people live full lives; it doesn’t automatically mean your dad’s path or his timeline."

"On having children — you have real options. You can conceive naturally accepting the chance; there are tests in pregnancy; and there’s a route with IVF where embryos are checked so an unaffected one is chosen — the NHS funds that when certain criteria are met. The genetics team can talk you through all of these properly — no one will push you in any direction."

"I’ll refer you to the kidney specialists and to the genetics service so you get expert, unhurried advice. One thing to know: this condition can rarely affect blood vessels in the brain — so a sudden, worst-ever ‘thunderclap’ headache means call 999. Otherwise, let’s take this a step at a time, and come back whenever you need to."

f.learning: This is a genetic/chronic-disease counselling consultation about AUTOSOMAL DOMINANT POLYCYSTIC KIDNEY DISEASE (ADPKD). Explain the inheritance plainly: ADPKD (usually PKD1/PKD2) is dominant, so each child of an affected parent has a 50% chance of inheriting it — with her father affected, her prior risk is 50%, and a diagnosis is not certain. Discuss presymptomatic screening SENSITIVELY rather than assuming she wants it: renal ULTRASOUND is first-line, with age-dependent diagnostic criteria (and a normal scan in someone young does not fully exclude disease), and genetic testing is available; crucially counsel the implications — psychological impact, the RIGHT NOT TO KNOW, and, kept separate, insurance: under the Code on Genetic Testing and Insurance (2018) predictive genetic test results need not be disclosed below the financial limits, whereas a scan showing cysts is a medical finding insurers may ask about — supporting an autonomous decision. Outline what a diagnosis would mean: proactive BLOOD PRESSURE control (ACE inhibitor/ARB, renoprotective), eGFR/proteinuria monitoring, hydration and lifestyle, tolvaptan for selected rapidly-progressing cases (NICE TA358: CKD stage 2 or 3 at the start of treatment, specialist-initiated), and management of complications (cyst haemorrhage/infection, stones, pain) — framed realistically (many live full lives) rather than catastrophically. Know the EXTRA-RENAL features — liver cysts, intracranial ANEURYSMS (with thunderclap-headache red-flag advice and consideration of screening in higher-risk groups), mitral valve prolapse, diverticular disease, hernias. Address reproductive options non-directively — natural conception with 50% risk, prenatal diagnosis, PREIMPLANTATION GENETIC TESTING with IVF, donor gametes, adoption — emphasising pre-conception counselling, and refer to NEPHROLOGY and CLINICAL GENETICS. Throughout, acknowledge the fear, pace the information, support autonomy without steering, and safety-net.

knowledge.guideline: KDIGO ADPKD guideline 2025 (international) · NICE TA358 (tolvaptan, 2015) · NICE NG203 (chronic kidney disease, 2021) · HM Government and ABI Code on Genetic Testing and Insurance (2018)
knowledge.summary: A child of a parent with ADPKD has a 1 in 2 chance of inheriting it. Offer information and choice about testing rather than testing by default, check blood pressure, and refer to clinical genetics for predictive testing and reproductive options.

points.t: ADPKD is autosomal dominant, usually from PKD1 or PKD2 variants. Each child of an affected parent has a 50% chance of inheriting it. Her prior risk is 50%, and so would be each of her children’s if she were affected.

Renal ultrasound is the usual first test in at-risk adults. The age-dependent unified ultrasound criteria (Pei 2009, international) require at least 3 cysts in total at age 15 to 39. A normal scan in a young adult does not fully exclude ADPKD, particularly with PKD2 disease; genetic testing gives a clearer answer when a family variant is known.

Predictive testing is her choice, including the choice not to know. Under the Code on Genetic Testing and Insurance, insurers cannot require a predictive genetic test, and results need not be disclosed below the financial limits (Huntington’s disease is the only listed exception). A scan showing cysts is a medical finding, which insurers may ask about.

Regular blood pressure checks and control, eGFR and urine ACR monitoring, and specialist care. NICE TA358: tolvaptan is an option for adults with CKD stage 2 or 3 at the start of treatment and evidence of rapidly progressing disease, started by specialists. Progression varies; many people keep good kidney function for decades.

Liver cysts, intracranial aneurysm (KDIGO 2025, international: screening is considered with a family history of aneurysm or subarachnoid haemorrhage), mitral valve prolapse and hernias. A sudden, worst-ever headache needs 999.

Natural conception accepting the risk, prenatal diagnosis, preimplantation genetic testing with IVF when the family variant is known, donor gametes or adoption. Clinical genetics provides non-directive counselling; NHS funding for preimplantation testing has eligibility criteria.

model.text: Hello Lucy, I’m Dr Lee. What would you like to talk about today?

My dad’s just started dialysis — he’s got polycystic kidney disease, and so did my gran. I feel fine, but it’s scared me. Do I have it? Should I be tested? And the big one — my partner and I have talked about kids, and I’m terrified of passing it on.

I’m sorry about your dad; that must be a hard thing to watch. You’ve raised three big questions: whether you might have it, testing, and children. We can go through each, at your pace. Which matters most to you today?
model.why: Acknowledges, structures and lets her prioritise

model.text: Probably the kids. But I need to understand the rest first.
What do you already know about the condition, from your dad’s experience?
That the kidneys fill with cysts and stop working. And that it’s in families. That’s about it.
Has anyone in the family had a brain aneurysm or a bleed in the brain?
model.why: Family history relevant to aneurysm screening

model.text: Not that I know of.
And for you — any headaches, pain in your side or back, blood in your urine, or infections? Has your blood pressure ever been checked?
None of that. I don’t think my blood pressure has been checked in years.
How are you coping with your dad starting dialysis?
Badly, honestly. I keep picturing myself in that chair. That’s why I’m here.
That makes sense. What worries you most — your own health or your future children’s?
Both. But mostly I don’t want my child to go through what dad has.
And what were you hoping would come out of today?
To know my chances, and what I can actually do.

This condition is passed on in what we call a dominant way. Each child of someone who has it has a one in two chance of inheriting it. So your chance is 50% — which also means it’s just as likely you don’t have it.
model.why: Explains inheritance plainly and balances the risk

model.text: Fifty-fifty. Okay.

You can find out, and there are two ways. A kidney scan looks for cysts, though at your age a clear scan doesn’t completely rule it out. A genetic test can give a clearer answer, especially if your dad’s gene change is known. Some people want to know now; some prefer to wait. There’s no wrong answer.
Are there downsides to knowing?

It’s worth thinking about. There’s the emotional side of knowing. There’s insurance: under the UK code, insurers can’t make you take a predictive genetic test, and in most cases you don’t have to tell them the result. A scan showing cysts is treated differently, as a medical finding. The genetics team can go through this in detail.
I didn’t know that. And if I do have it?

Then we’d keep a close eye on blood pressure and kidney function and treat blood pressure early, because that protects the kidneys. For some people whose kidneys decline quickly, there’s a specialist medicine that slows it. It varies a lot even within families — having it doesn’t mean following your dad’s timeline.
model.why: Realistic outline of management and prognosis

model.text: About children: you have real options. You could conceive naturally and accept the chance. There are tests during pregnancy. And there’s IVF with testing of embryos, so an unaffected one is chosen — that needs the family gene change to be known, and NHS funding has criteria. Some people consider donor eggs or adoption.
I didn’t know the embryo thing was possible.

The genetics service can talk it through with you and your partner, without pushing you either way. I’d suggest a referral there. Whatever you decide about testing, can we check your blood pressure and a urine sample? That’s sensible for anyone your age with this family history, and it doesn’t commit you to anything.
model.why: Non-directive referral and a low-stakes first step

model.text: Yes, I’m happy with that. I think I do want to know, but I want to talk to the genetics people first.
That sounds a very sensible way to do it. I’ll refer you, and if you choose testing, we’ll arrange it and involve the kidney specialists if it shows anything.

One thing to know: rarely this condition affects blood vessels in the brain. A sudden, severe, worst-ever headache means calling 999. Otherwise, book the blood pressure check with the nurse, and come back any time — this is a decision you can take over time.
model.why: Aneurysm red flag, next step and open door

model.text: To make sure I’ve been clear, what will you tell your partner tonight?
That it’s fifty-fifty, that I can choose whether and how to be tested, and that there are ways to have children without passing it on. I feel less panicky.

social.t: Watching a parent start dialysis shapes how she hears risk. Acknowledge the grief and fear before giving numbers.
Reproductive decisions involve her partner; offer joint genetics counselling.

legal.t: Code on Genetic Testing and Insurance (HM Government and ABI, 2018): insurers will not require predictive genetic tests; results need not be disclosed below the financial limits, and Huntington’s disease is the only listed exception.
Her father’s genetic result belongs to him. Using it to guide her testing needs his consent (GMC Confidentiality, 2017).

professional.t: Offer information and options; support her decision about testing and reproduction without steering (GMC Decision making and consent, 2020).
Declining predictive testing is a valid choice. Blood pressure checks can still be offered.

community.t: The PKD Charity and Kidney Care UK provide information and peer support for families.

pitfalls.intro: This is a counselling station. It is lost by testing by default, inaccurate facts about scans and insurance, and steering reproductive choices.

items.fail: Arranging an ultrasound straight away “to rule it out”.
items.why: Assumes she wants predictive information, and a clear scan at 24 does not fully exclude ADPKD.
items.fix: Offer testing as a choice, explain the limits of a young scan, and refer to clinical genetics.

items.fail: Warning her that any test result must be declared to insurers.
items.why: The Code on Genetic Testing and Insurance says otherwise for predictive genetic tests below the limits.
items.fix: Give the accurate position, and note that a scan finding is handled differently.

items.fail: Answering the question about children with “that’s one for the specialists”.
items.why: Her main concern goes unaddressed in the consultation.
items.fix: Outline the options in plain words, then refer for detailed, non-directive counselling.

items.fail: Suggesting she might avoid having children.
items.why: Directive counselling breaches autonomy and loses Relating marks.
items.fix: Present options neutrally and ask what matters to her.

items.fail: Delivering inheritance, testing, management, extra-renal features and reproductive options in one monologue.
items.fix: Let her choose priorities, pace the information, and check understanding with teach-back.

items.fail: No safety-net because she is well.
items.why: Thunderclap headache advice matters in at-risk relatives.
items.fix: Give the 999 message and book a blood pressure check.

timeMap.d: Three questions arrive at once. Name them and let her choose the order.
What she knows, symptoms, BP history, family history of aneurysm; how she is coping with her father’s dialysis.
50% risk; scan vs genetic test; right not to know; insurance code; what a diagnosis would mean.
Natural, prenatal, IVF with embryo testing, donor, adoption; clinical genetics referral; BP and urine check.
Thunderclap headache is 999; open door; teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Books an ultrasound without asking if she wants to know; says a normal scan rules it out; gives wrong or alarming insurance advice; tells her not to have children or ignores the question; no referral.
wordPics.pass: Explains 50% risk; offers scan or genetic testing as a choice; outlines management if diagnosed; lists reproductive options; refers to clinical genetics; checks BP.
wordPics.exc: All of that, plus: explains a clear young scan does not fully exclude; gives accurate insurance information; balances hope with honesty about variable progression; stays non-directive; includes her partner; checks understanding with teach-back.

avoid.dont: “Let’s get you a scan to put your mind at rest.”
avoid.instead: “You can find out if you want to — but it’s your choice, and there are things worth thinking through first.”
avoid.why: Assumes she wants predictive testing and implies a normal scan is conclusive.

avoid.dont: “You’d have to tell insurers if you had a genetic test.”
avoid.instead: “Under the UK code, in most cases you don’t have to disclose a predictive genetic test result.”
avoid.why: Incorrect and may deter a test she wants.

avoid.dont: “If you have it, you’ll probably end up like your dad.”
avoid.instead: “It varies a lot, even in the same family, and early blood-pressure control helps.”
avoid.why: Catastrophising removes hope and is not accurate.

Natural conception accepting the risk, prenatal diagnosis, preimplantation genetic testing with IVF when the family variant is known, donor gametes or adoption. Clinical genetics provides non-directive counselling; NHS funding for preimplantation testing has eligibility criteria.

social.t: Watching a parent start dialysis shapes how she hears risk. Acknowledge the grief and fear before giving numbers.
Reproductive decisions involve her partner; offer joint genetics counselling.

legal.t: Code on Genetic Testing and Insurance (HM Government and ABI, 2018): insurers will not require predictive genetic tests; results need not be disclosed below the financial limits, and Huntington’s disease is the only listed exception.
Her father’s genetic result belongs to him. Using it to guide her testing needs his consent (GMC Confidentiality, 2017).

professional.t: Offer information and options; support her decision about testing and reproduction without steering (GMC Decision making and consent, 2020).
Declining predictive testing is a valid choice. Blood pressure checks can still be offered.

community.t: The PKD Charity and Kidney Care UK provide information and peer support for families.

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This is a counselling station. It is lost by testing by default, inaccurate facts about scans and insurance, and steering reproductive choices.

items.fail: Arranging an ultrasound straight away “to rule it out”.
items.why: Assumes she wants predictive information, and a clear scan at 24 does not fully exclude ADPKD.
items.fix: Offer testing as a choice, explain the limits of a young scan, and refer to clinical genetics.

items.fail: Warning her that any test result must be declared to insurers.
items.why: The Code on Genetic Testing and Insurance says otherwise for predictive genetic tests below the limits.
items.fix: Give the accurate position, and note that a scan finding is handled differently.

items.fail: Answering the question about children with “that’s one for the specialists”.
items.why: Her main concern goes unaddressed in the consultation.
items.fix: Outline the options in plain words, then refer for detailed, non-directive counselling.

items.fail: Suggesting she might avoid having children.
items.why: Directive counselling breaches autonomy and loses Relating marks.
items.fix: Present options neutrally and ask what matters to her.

items.fail: Delivering inheritance, testing, management, extra-renal features and reproductive options in one monologue.
items.fix: Let her choose priorities, pace the information, and check understanding with teach-back.

items.fail: No safety-net because she is well.
items.why: Thunderclap headache advice matters in at-risk relatives.
items.fix: Give the 999 message and book a blood pressure check.
